utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Carter, I've asked for the witness to be withdrawn briefly to clarify certain things which I endeavoured to clarify through the Legal Officer this morning but was unable to get an answer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, for this we should go into private session if you're going into any detail.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like you to listen carefully to what I have to say to you, and when I've read this short statement, I wish you to simply say: I do. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin with the witness, I'd like to bring the Court's attention that this witness will be dealing with paragraphs of the indictment, specifically paragraph 72 (C), paragraph 77 (B), and paragraph 75 (F), along with schedule (F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, will you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Mustafa Draga.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Draga, your name has been spelled several different ways through the course of this -- these proceedings. So you -- can you confirm for us the first -- your name -- excuse me, the spelling of your first name as well as your last name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: My name is written Mustafa Draga.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So there is an A on the end of your first name as well as your last name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript, Ms. Carter, you'll see the way the name has been produced, and I think we'll all accept that that's an accurate reproduction of how the name should be presented unless you think there's something wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, we're here today to develop the story of what happened to you in March of 1999. However, before that, there apparently were some issues that occurred in your village in 1998. Can you tell us how long you were living in Lecina village.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Since I was born. All my life I lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you raise a family in that village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. I lived there with my family, in the village I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many members of your family lived with you in that village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Now -- I used to have 20 members, but ten of them do not live there. They are in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May I take it that it is you and your wife and some children. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And are these adult children?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In 1998, you previously indicated that the village made a change for the worse. Can you describe for me what occurred in 1998 that began to make you and your family members fearful?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We were scared because some went to Ulcinj. I went to Mitrovica; some took to the mountains. They stopped us in the street. They beat us, they maltreat us. Nobody like to leave his home.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At that time, were there any sort of check-points or anything of that nature set up in or near your village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Not in the village. In Junik was the closest one, Mitrovica, in other place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that you had gone to Mitrovica. Had you passed through this check-point that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. I passed through the mountains. That was the route I took. I didn't dare pass through the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated there was maltreatment to the villagers at this time. What type of maltreatment were you subjected to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When they caught us in the street, they beat us. They maltreated us. People were obliged to leave their homes and spend most of the time in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was there any type of shelling or anything like that in the villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a live witness, and I'd ask my friend not to lead him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter? No, please don't answer -- please don't answer that question. We have an objection to it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I will try to curtail the questions so that they do not appear to be leading in their nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, you'll need to rephrase that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have anything else that you believe the Court needs to know about 1998 in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: My village was not burned in 1998; it was torched in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let's begin in 1999, around the time of the NATO bombings. What, if anything, extraordinary was beginning to occur on March 25th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They started to set fire on houses on the 25th of March and shelling the village. On the 26th, I went higher to -- to a place which was called Leqine. I with my wife stayed in the basement for four, five hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you right now and stay with the 25th. You said on the 25th there began to be shelling within your village. Who was shelling at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Who could have done that other than the Serbian police and army?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why do you think it is the Serbian police and army who did this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Because they did what they wanted, to ethnically cleanse the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On March 25th, were you aware of where the shelling was come from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: From the direction of Padalishte and Leqine, not more than a kilometre away. This is why we left the house. From where we went -- from the place we went to, we could see very well the village being burned and shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you're saying "the village," are you referring to Leqine or another village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It was another neighbourhood we were staying. The village was Leqine, at the edge of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me which villages or which locations were being shelled on March 25th?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Padalishte and part of Leqine, half of it. The other half was shelled on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When the shelling was occurring, was it being isolated within the villages or did it -- had a broader spectrum?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They shelled all places. First they shelled Leqine, set fire to it, within a 10 kilometres radius.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated on March 26th you and your wife went to another area. What is that area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Izbica village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What, if anything, was occurring in Izbica at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Nothing happened on that day, but it did -- something happened on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why did you choose Izbica as being a location you would feel safe?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I chose Izbica because I felt it was safer. There was a forest nearby you could take refuge in. There was no place we could take shelter in my place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long did you have this period of safety in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: How long did I stay, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: On the 26th we went there. On the 27th we stayed there. On the 28th the massacre took place. Then I stayed there during all the time that the fighting continued. Then my sons left, some went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you'd indicated that on the 27th you were still in the village. Were you in the village proper or were you somewhere near the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: In the village, inside the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you in some sort of housing, or were you in the open air?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Other people stayed in their homes. We stayed outside, in the mountains, in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the mountains and in the forest, can you approximate for us how many people were sheltering there with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Two or three at the most. They couldn't dare stay there in larger groups because when they shelled they didn't want to be hit by the shells if they stayed in large groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you say -- stay broken off into these smaller groups, or at some point did you become a larger group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were no larger groups anywhere because they didn't dare stay in large groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Just prior to the massacre, where were you staying with your family?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I was in Izbica with my family; from the 26th we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What area were you in at the point that you became engaged with the -- the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: In Izbica village. I was there when the Serbian forces entered the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you in some sort of structure or were you in an open-air area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When the Serbian forces entered, we were in a meadow with some other people. Then we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We raised four white flags.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why did you go into this field, into this meadow?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We rallied there together, all of us, because we believed they wouldn't kill us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "we," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were many families from the municipality of Klina. There were over 20.000 people gathered there, at the least. The sons went to the mountains. I was there with my other members.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the sons went into the mountains, who was left within the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Many people remained there and many of those who were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In this field were there men, women, children? Who was in the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. Who else could be there? Men, women, children.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was the difference between the men who left for the mountains and the men who remained in the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Because they were elderly men and they thought that they wouldn't be killed, because if they knew they would be killed they too would have taken to the mountains because the mountain was not far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long had you been staying in this field prior to the Serbian forces arriving?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: From the 27th to the 28th until 10.00 or 11.00 - I am not sure about the exact time - until the Serbian forces came.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were in the field, what were the living conditions like at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Deplorable. What could I say? It was raining -- it was raining and mud there. I cannot describe worse conditions than those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you have any sort of shelter or were you in the open air?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We were in the open air all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the first time that you saw the Serbian forces arrive.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: What can I describe, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you describe when you saw the Serbian forces when you were in the field. Can you describe that event.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When the Serbian forces came to the meadow, they came from all sides, and they asked us for money. Whoever had money on them, they gave them to the Serbian forces. They asked me, too, but I had no money to give them so they gave me a blow here. They started to divide men from women --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to explore with you for a moment who these Serbian forces were. Can you please describe what they looked like who surrounded you in the field.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They were police and army forces. We didn't even dare look up at them to see how they looked like because they were behaving very badly towards us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did you know that they were police and army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Because of their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What kind of clothes were they in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What colour was the camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Like green, grass green. I'm sure they know who gave them those clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were all of the members who surrounded you in the field, were they all in green or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The ones who were closer to us I could see because, as I said, we were too afraid to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your younger years you actually served in compulsory military service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say or not that you would be familiar with uniforms due to that service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I did my military service in the 1960s, so many years have passed and the uniforms have been changed. When I was doing my military service, we had other military uniforms. There is a great difference between that time and now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So once the Serbian soldiers had surrounded you in the field -- can you tell me, how big was this field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Two or three hectares large.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And as the men in the green uniforms were approaching, were they right next to each other, shoulder to shoulder? Were they arm's width away? Or were they much further away from each other?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They came there as they wanted, you know, because they were not afraid of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm trying to learn is approximately how many soldiers surrounded you in the wood? Or in the field, pardon.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: This I don't know. I know that there were many.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you say that there were more than 10?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: What are you saying 10? They were 2 or 300, I think. Or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After they surrounded you in the wood, you indicated they began taking money. Were they taking money from the men only? From the women? Or from everybody?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I saw them asking money from the men, but I couldn't see what everyone was doing because, as I said, we were many people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When they began asking money from the men, were you still within the crowd of the women or had you been separated from the women?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They had separated us when they asked us for money. But they asked us for money even before they started separating us. They threatened to burn our houses and take away our tractors if we didn't give them money.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After they requested money, what did they do next?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: After that, they separated the men from the women. They told the men to sit on the right side and asked the rest to go towards Turiqevc. They asked us to line up, asked us for money, insulted us, and started to throw our caps at us. Then one group they sent to the west. They sent us to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, when you're referring to these two groups being sent to the west and to the right side, are you referring to the men only or are you referring to the men and the women being these two groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. They told the women to go towards Turiqevc, while the men -- one of the group of men was sent to the west and I was in the group that was sent in the direction of the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when the women went to Turiqevc, were there any men with them whatsoever or were all the men taken out of that group and brought into the two groups you refer to going east and west?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't see any men in that group of women that day. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When the men were separated from the women, how many men were there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I couldn't count them. I didn't dare look around, but there were a lot of men. I thought maybe 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were separated into the two groups, how many men in uniform were with each group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When we were taken in -- to the eastern direction and were told to go to the site of the mountain, we were lined up. We were told to walk two abreast. They were insulting us, and they shot at us. And people fell down. I fell down. Hajriz Draga fell on me. He called for help. I didn't have any water or anything to help him. I stayed here lying down for some time, and then I got up and went towards the mountain, And I didn't dare get out of the forest of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you said that you were lined up and walked two abreast to the point of the massacre, was it the same -- were you being escorted or were you walking alone?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They were accompanying us. That's where the massacre happened. People were walking when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you say "they were accompanying us." Is it the same men in green camouflage uniforms, different men, or a combination of the two?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I have come here to tell the truth. When they were escorting us, I didn't dare to look at them, what kind of clothes they were wearing. They then shot at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the man looked like who separated you into the two groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When we were separated into two groups, their uniforms were camouflage. One of them was wearing something like a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were there any other uniforms that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember that there were any where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You'd also indicated that when you were in the lines that they were throwing your hats at you. Can you please tell us what is the significance -- what is the insult there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, you know, that's an insult. They were playing with our hats. They were beating us. Why did they play with the hats as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I am an Albanian, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, do the Serbs who lived in this area, do they wear these hats or is this strictly something of your group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The hats are worn by Albanians only. My father used to wear it. My grandfather used to wear it. My sons don't wear it anymore, but the Serbs don't wear this kind of hat we call plis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As they were beating you, were they saying anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. They shouted abuse at us, at Rugova, Thaqi, all kinds of insults.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then you indicated that they began to walk you somewhere. Can you please describe to the Court in detail what that final walk before the massacre was like.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We were at the meadow. We were separated, men from women. We were told to line up. We -- they asked us questions. They insulted us. As I told you, they played with our hats. When they came to me, they told us to go towards the east. There was another group who went to the west. Milazim was there. We were told to go up the mountain. They were insulting us at that time saying: F your mothers. And they told: Return. Come back, come back. And we were turning around, and they shot at us. I will never forget that. Only the day I die will this be erased from my mind. I lived this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As they were shooting at you, how many men, if you know, died that day in your group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know how many were killed, because from the 28th to the 31st of March we didn't dare go there again. But when we buried them, we counted that there were 147.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You had indicated previously that when you fell to the ground, Hajriz Draga fell on top of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how long were you required to lie in a field of dead men with a friend lying on top of you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: About 30 minutes, at the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was happening around you in those 30 minutes that you did not feel safe enough to be able to leave that massacre site?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When they executed us, they went to the meadow. But we didn't know that they had gone to the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Because I was afraid to look around where they were because I was afraid also that they would kill me. Again, start shooting again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After those 30 minutes, you had indicated that you were able to leave the massacre site. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I went about 15 -- 50 metres away, to the mountain, and I stayed there. I was afraid to go back and look at the bodies. I didn't dare go and look at Hajriz, how he was or what his situation was, because the police and army was right there, a little further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you crawled into the woods, were there any other survivors of your group of men?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Musli Hajra from Klina, he took my hand and took me to the mountain. We stayed there. He was killed a month later. He told me: You have to crawl. Come here, come here. You have to crawl because everything is burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you see the burnings that he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We saw from there, from the mountain -- we could only see the smoke, nothing else, and the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, remind me of the name of the person who fell on top of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hajriz Draga. He was from my neighbourhood. He was also a cousin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he killed or did he survive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was alive at the beginning, but he died later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he able to leave the spot at which he fell or did he die there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he died there, on the spot where he was executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In anticipation of what I believe Your Honours are trying to learn --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you'd indicated that Hajriz, spelled H-a-j-r-i-z, was the man who fell on top of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you went into the woods, did you find other survivors of the massacre within the woods?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Hajzer Draga, he was a survivor as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And Hajzer is H-a-j-z-e-r. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, Draga.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And that man from the -- Klina is different from the man who fell upon you during the massacre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Hajzer and Hajriz are cousins together, but they're also cousins of mine. We're all relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who else did you meet? You'd indicated you met Musli Hajra, now Hajzer Draga. Can you remember anybody else that survived and you met in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody else. I stayed with Hajzer and Musli Hajra for three or four days in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were the conditions like that you were supposed to survive in within those mountains?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine, no food, no water in the mountains. We were -- nothing was there for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you'd also indicated that you were able to see some smoke from which you believe were burnings in a village. Which village was that that you saw the smoke coming from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The smoke came from the village of Izbica where the massacre happened. Also, the tractors, I believe, were burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the geography a bit of that region. How -- what type of elevation were you on in order to be able to see all these things?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: During the time we were there in the meadow, it was a flat area. When we went up to the area where the execution happened, it was about 20 metres higher from the meadow. And we could see the houses and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You'd indicated that you had to remain in the mountains for several days. When did the Serbian forces leave?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The Serb forces left and went to Vojnik and Broj. They left on the 31st of March. On the 30th in the evening -- on the 31st, because they had left, we went and buried the victims in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When it was time to bury the dead, were there people beyond just those that had been massacred that had to be buried on that day?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We buried the people who were killed there. They killed even a man who was 105 years old.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the person. I believe it was Zade Draga.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you indicate for us who the 105-year-old man was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Zade Dragaj. She was a woman. It was Hajzer's mother -- she was Hajzer's mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were any other women killed during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. There were other woman who were killed en route. We found some in Jashanica, one called Ashe Dragaj, and woman from other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a woman by the name of Zoje Osmana?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, because my cousin married her daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of her fate?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: She was paralyzed and she was burned in the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where was she burned in the tractor?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: At the meadow in Izbica, where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was this at or near the time of the massacre in which you survived?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The same day of the massacre, both the houses and the tractors were burned that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did anybody die along with Ms. Osmana at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were other paralyzed people, Shaban Muslia, Zeqir Salihi and one woman from Vojnik. These people had remained on the tractors.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did they meet the same fate as Ms. Osmana?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is it my understanding based on your previous comments that you were one of the members who had to bury the dead?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in the funeral, and my sons as well. They carried the bodies on the tractors, on their tractors. Everybody helped who could.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many people were buried that day?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: How could I know, but I think it was 147 on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When the bodies were buried, was there any procedure or any marcations that were given to the gravesites?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They put some planks on the graves with numbers, 1, 2, and 3, and so on, and they buried them without coffins, just in their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, were there other KLA members present at the time of these burials?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were, yes. They took part in the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So how did the KLA become involved in this funeral?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know how it came about for them to be there, but there were so many people. And they had to be buried because the bodies were decomposing. People were not able to recognise their cousins, their relatives, even their fathers. Only the clothes they could recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the burial, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: After the burial, we went to the mountain. On the 10th of May, three people were killed in Izbica. And on the 14th -- on the 11th, 14 people were killed again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How do you know that these individuals were killed on the 10th and the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know because I was in the mountains and I took part in their burial. I know that on the 11th my wife and my daughter and my daughter-in-law were told to go towards Albania, the same day that that massacre happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who told them to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The Serbian police and army. The ones that carried out the massacre were the ones that told them to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you have to survive within the woods and mountains around this region?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I stayed there until the day when they exhumed the bodies. Before they exhumed the bodies, there was a lot of shelling and I went to Izbica again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So that we can get a time-frame, when did they exhume the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They started exhuming them on the 28th of May. I don't know for how long it lasted, four or five days, and nobody -- none of the bodies remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, this material was not disclosed to us in the 65 ter summary. I presume it falls under the same guidelines as the decision yesterday. I just wanted to have our objection on the record. I presume we'll proceed the same way we did with the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Ivetic. We -- the problem is, in this case, I don't have the 65 ter summary in front of me to know whether, in fact, it really is out with it. But in view of the events of yesterday and what we said the Defence could do if there were any difficulties presented by this information coming to light at this stage, we'll follow the same course because it -- it fits into the same area. It's an extension of the evidence that the witness was known to be giving. However, we do make it clear that when evidence, plainly outwith that envisaged with the 65 ter summary, is to be presented by Prosecution and indeed Defence in due course, we expect an application to be made for leave to be extended beyond the anticipated areas. And that course should be followed in all future situations. But please carry on with your questions, which we will allow you to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you'd indicated that on June -- I'm sorry, on May 28th, approximately, the bodies of Izbica were exhumed. Did you see those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, we did not. Because first they shelled the area; then after that they exhumated the bodies. We knew from the day they shelled the place what was going to happen. They exhumed the bodies during the day, and at night they didn't work. When they took away all the bodies, I saw with my own eyes that not a single one was left there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "they shelled" and "they exhumed," can you tell us who "they" are?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They are the Serbian police and army, those who shot them. It was not the Albanians who did the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, prior to your family returning home in June, were you living in the mountains this entire time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, until the NATO forces entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At any time were you able to return to your home in Lecina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't even try to go back to it. Why should I? Everything razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that it was razed to the ground. Does that mean that you were able to see at some point what happened to your home?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Everything was burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was just your home burned or were there others?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I saw that only once when it was burned, and after that -- the first time it was burned. After that, I didn't go back. No house was left intact in Leqine. Three times they entered the village and set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You've also indicated that there were times in which you were Izbica. Did the homes in Izbica face the same fate?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Only a few houses remained unburned, but the bulk were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I read that evidence as saying that after the witness left Leqine, which was the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He didn't go back at all. Is that how you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you understand it differently, you should seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, understandably you have never been able -- you were not able to live in your home again, but did you have an opportunity to go to Leqine and be able to see the place in which your home once stood?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I went once to see the house that was burned, and that was after the massacre. After that time, there was no reason for me to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in this order: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic and together with Branko Lukic and Ozren Ogrizovic, I represent Sreten Lukic in these proceedings. And today we have some questions for you to answer to clear up a few points in your testimony. Now, first of all, sir, do you speak or understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the region or valley where your home village is located, does that region have a name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The village is called Leqine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the village of Leqine, is that located in the so-called Drenica Valley?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And within this Drenica Valley, would it be accurate to state that in 1998 and 1999 the so-called UCK or KLA were present and active in this valley?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were a few KLA members. I never had a chance to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the Drenica Valley, isn't it a fact that in 1998 and early 1999, portions of that territory were in fact under the control of the UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We are not situated in the valley of Drenice but on the edge. Please understand me where we are situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. And my question is: Within that greater area surrounding your village, among the other villages that were there, wouldn't it be accurate to state that much of this area was controlled by the so-called UCK/KLA in 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, no. It was not under the control of the KLA. It did not control anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your home village of Leqine, in 1998 and 1999 there were some young men in that village who were members of the UCK/KLA. Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know who was. I know that there were a few, but I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with these few men that you state were members of the UCK/KLA in your village, was there any type of base or command post contained in the village for these men?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know nothing of that, and I was not even interested in knowing anything. I wanted to take care of my own business, my family, I mean, my own affairs. I was not interested in what KLA did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that you may not have been interested in what the KLA did, but did you observe or were you aware of, through other people in the village, the fact that the 145th Brigade of the so-called KLA was in fact based in and around your village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know that there was anything in my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, did it never worry you, because you were so concerned about the safety of your family, that the presence of the KLA in your village might actually put your family in danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It didn't do anything to me. I didn't have any danger coming to me from KLA. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you not think, however, that the Serb forces might attack the KLA in your village, and thus put other villagers in danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody knew that the Serbian forces would attack, and this is what happened because they were unequal as far as their armaments went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But perhaps if you had kicked the KLA out of your village, they wouldn't have attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on that day in Izbica there was no KLA presence. We were men, elderly men, as I told you, and they did what they did. They committed that bloodshed. Everyone knows that. But thank God now justice is being done and all the world can see what happened then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand entirely what you're saying about that event. I am not asking about that at the moment. I am asking a quite separate matter which is about the presence of the KLA in your village, and I'm really very anxious to know why it is you had no interest in whether they were there. That if you had shown an interest, perhaps you would have tried to do something about removing them and your family would have been safer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My family would have never been safe. Since 1997, when they put up those check-points, we always had problems. They beat my sons at the check-points, so we never felt safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you talk about when the forces of Serbia came to your region. Isn't it a fact that these forces came into the region in -- prior to 1999 for the express purpose of dealing with the threat posed by the KLA, who was operating in that area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't get your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Allow me to repeat it. Sir, you testified about the years prior to 1999. When you say in 1997 and 1998 that the forces of Serbia came to the region where your village is located, I'm asking you: Isn't it a fact that the reason that the Serbian forces came to that area was for the express purpose of dealing with the threat posed by the KLA who were present there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Serbian forces did -- didn't -- didn't come to my village before. They didn't come in 1997; they came in 1998. And as I said to you, whenever they saw you in the street they could beat you and insult you without you doing anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question, I believe, said, and I'm looking at the transcript to make sure, and it is accurate. I was asking you about the forces of Serbia that came to the region where your village is located, not specifically to your village. Isn't it a fact that in 1998 the forces that came, came as a direct response to the threat posed by the KLA who were operating in that region?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware, sir, that the UCK or KLA forces in the region where your village is located, that is to say, within Drenica, had at their disposal machine-guns, mortars, rocket-launchers, and other heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, within your village, sir, did many households in your village have any fire-arms or weapons at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I haven't seen that because the Serbian police collected the weapons before. They took me to Stanica and they beat me. They asked us for weapons, but we didn't have any weapons left because they collected the weapons before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, you've mentioned the Serbian police. Could you describe for me, please, the types of uniforms and insignia that these Serbian police that you just described wore at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They wore the police uniforms. I didn't pay any attention to that. My concern was to get away from them, and this -- that was my only concern, how to find the easiest way to get away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've just used the terminology "they wore the police uniforms." I need for you to describe for us what that terminology means. What are the police uniforms? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The police used to wear dark clothes. They came and took me at my home. I was outside in the yard. It didn't even enter my mind to look at their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "dark clothes," do you know what colour?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I can't describe the colour. You may know better. I am telling you that they took me to the police station and beat me, and my household new nothing about that. I didn't look at the clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've heard that, sir. How is it that you know that these were Serbian policemen if you did not look at the clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I knew that because we knew who the policemen were because they had some uniform on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so you do have knowledge of the uniform. I'm simply asking you to describe the uniform so that we can proceed with other areas of this examination.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It was not entirely black and entirely green, but as I told you they keep changing their uniforms every day. I didn't even think of looking at the uniform when they took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, these people, did they have any badges or emblems on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't see that. They put me in that room in the police station, and then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I'll move along. Now, returning to the moment of the activities of the UCK/KLA in 1998 and 1999, were any members of your family or any other close relatives members of the UCK/KLA in either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There was no one from my family in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you familiar with an individual named Shaban Draga or Shaban Dragaj from the same village as you are located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you -- have you ever heard of a Sadik Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it a fact that Sadik Xhemajli was a local UCK/KLA commander who participated in the funeral in Izbica that we'll talk about later?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It is true that he took part in the funeral, but as to your question whether he was a commander or not, this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall giving a statement to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal in the year 1999, in November of 1999, wherein you identified Sadik Xhemajli as the local KLA commander in addition to the person who organised -- one of the people that organised the funeral in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It is true that I said he took part in the funeral, but I have not said that he was a commander. That must be wrong. Had I known, I would have said. I remember I said the first time that he participated in the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can move for a moment to the other individual that I mentioned, this Shaban Draga, how is it that you know him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Shaban Draga is from the same neighbourhood of mine, but he lives in Mitrovica for some 40 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there a younger Shaban Draga who would have been around 22 to 27 years of age in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There is no other Shaban in Leqine, not by the last name of Draga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, is this a suitable time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I can interrupt here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- on the transcript at page 31, line 7, the answer tails off as: "Then I." What I heard the witness say was: "And beat me."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter may explain that he said: "Had I known, I would have told you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you anything. I'm just recording something for the transcript. We'll now adjourn for 20 minutes and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Draga, we left off talking about a Shaban Draga or Dragaj. Isn't it a fact that this individual, Shaban Dragaj, was also involved in the organisation of the funeral at Izbica on March the 31st, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I did not see Shaban there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask for a point of clarification, as it became at issue as to whether we were talking about the man, the Shaban Draga, that this gentleman has known for 40 some odd years or the Shaban Draga that was alluded to who was approximately 22 to 27 years old, make the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yeah, you're probably right, but since he's already made it clear he only knows one Shaban Dragaj, it could only be a question about the older one. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It could be a question about a younger one, too, which I will hopefully clear up with the next question, Your Honour. I don't know. I'll find out from the answer with the next two questions, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with an Abedin Dragaj from Leqine?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know Abedin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Abedin, born in 1976, is your nephew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, he's the son of my brother, if you're talking about the same one I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I am, sir. Now, I'd like to refresh your recollection about whether you know any other Shaban Dragajs by putting forth to you that your nephew, Abedin Dragaj, gave a sworn statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on April 24th, 1999, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, this witness cannot be refreshed from another person's transcript or from his statement, especially in that that person is not coming before the Court. It's an inappropriate recollect -- refreshment of recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not using a document, since I think we discussed that that would not be a means of being able to do so with this witness, but I believe that a witness can be confronted upon cross-examination and refreshed with any fact. I mean, his answer will be whatever his answer is, and it may help me, it may not. I'm entitled to ask that question, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Ms. Carter, what's happening is he's being confronted with something said by another person. Now, that can be done without reference to who that person is and when he said it, but it's helpful to everyone, I would have thought, if in addition to the statement that's allegedly made, information is also given to us about the source. So I will repel that objection. Please continue with the question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the sake of the witness I think I'll start at the beginning so that there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to try and refresh your recollection as to whether you know of any other Shaban Dragajs, other than the one you have described as being in Mitrovica, by putting forth to you the fact that Abedin Dragaj gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, a sworn statement, on April 24th, 1999, in which he identifies a Shaban Draga, that is to say an UCK officer, who was present in Izbica, in the woods, on the time period of the 26th through the 27th of March, 1999, with him. Does that refresh your recollection as to the fact that there is another Shaban Dragaj or that the Shaban Dragaj that you know is an officer in the UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I told you earlier that there is no Shaban Dragaj in Lecina. I don't think there is another Shaban in other neighbourhoods as well, let alone Shaban Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was your nephew, Abedin, in Izbica at the time that you testified to earlier, that is to say the 26th or 27th of March, the time period when you were in Izbica as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Abedin was not with me. He was in the mountains somewhere. I don't know where he was. He was not there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But he was in the mountains surrounding Izbica [Realtime transcript read in error, "I see details"], in the forest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: In the mountains, somewhere, I don't know whether in Tushile, Rakinica, but he wasn't with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I ask my next question, I'm alerted to a problem in the transcript with my last question. At line 25 of page 35, the transcripts states: "But he was in the mountains surrounding I see details." I believe the "I see details" should be Izbica, which is clear, but I just wanted to catch it sooner rather than later for clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, isn't it a fact that during the 26th, 27th, and, I would posit, even the 28th of March, 1999, that there were many KLA combatants in the forests and the mountains surrounding Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It's not true, because I don't hear -- I didn't hear any fighting. There were soldiers, I'm not denying that, but there were only a few of them, just a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe earlier you had stated that there were no KLA in Izbica. How do you account for this change in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Not in Izbica, in the mountains. As I said, that day in Izbica where I was, there were no fighters. There were no guns. I couldn't hear any gun-shots or anything. And I take full responsibility when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could again refresh your recollection with the sworn statement of your nephew, and I'll read a section of his statement for you. "I decided to move my family to Izbica partly because Izbica was situated in a valley and was therefore less exposed to the Serb guns and partly because there was a greater UCK presence there." Does that refresh your recollection as to the nature of the UCK forces that were in Izbica at the time that you went there with others from your village?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I would object to this type of recollection -- refreshment of recollection. As the Defence counsel is able to put to this witness his case, what has been clear by this testimony is that this witness was not in the same area as his cousin -- or his nephew. He's said that. So for him to be held accountable for another person's perspective is completely inappropriate. It is not as if they were both in Izbica at the same time and seeing two different things; they are in two separate places addressing separate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what would you say he should ask him?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would say that he would ask him: Was there fight -- let's see, the question was that Izbica was in a valley, therefore less exposed to Serb guns. He can certainly ask that. Was there a great UCK presence there? He could certainly ask that. To somehow impose the knowledge of his nephew on him is completely inappropriate. He can certainly have the questions made to him, but his answers should stand and not have it appear as if he's given inconsistent statements. And the way it is being done appears as if he is giving inconsistent statements as opposed to two different people giving their own perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's treating us as assuming he's responsible for what his son -- his nephew has said, and obviously we would make no such assumption. But it's not uncommon for cross-examination of this nature to be based on: My information is that there was a greater UCK presence in Izbica. And I doubt if there's any fundamentally wrong with this, but it just doesn't come over properly, Mr. Ivetic. It's -- I think in a different context with a jury, it would undoubtedly not be allowed because it's capable of confusing the situation of the witness's own recollection and what other people have said. And I think it would be much more helpful to us if we just cut to the chase and just cut out all the detailed reference to this other statement, when in fact what you're putting to him is a very simple point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that people from your village of Lecina left that village on or around the 25th of March, 1999, to go to Izbica because there was a greater UCK presence in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll ask you another question about Izbica in particular. Isn't it a fact that in Izbica -- first of all, Izbica has a lower part and an upper part of the village. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is it a fact that whereas the -- strike that. Isn't it a fact that the upper part of Izbica village on and about the 25th and 26th of March, 1999, was in fact held by the KLA and that they had staged a defensive point there to combat with the other forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: When the civilians in Izbica returned from Tushile to the lower part of the village, isn't it a fact that it was the UCK fighters that dispersed into the woods and into the mountain surrounding Izbica, the same men you previously described as just the young males from the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see soldiers in the mountains where the families where. Maybe they were farther away, but I did not see them. If I had seen them, I would have told you so. If they had been there that day, maybe somebody would have put up a fight or something, but nobody shot any rifle or anything at that -- on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the UCK fighters, did they -- you said you did not see any soldiers, but isn't it a fact that the UCK fighters often wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I did not see any in civilian clothes. I believe that the KLA had KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could return to your village of Leqina again, prior to the time you left for Izbica, that is as of March 1999, were there any ethnic Serb civilians in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, the Serbs left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can direct your attention to the time period of early 1998. At that point in time, wasn't there in fact a part of your village called Smigic where there was a predominantly Serb -- where there were predominantly Serb households located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serbs living in Smigic, but they left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about these Serbs that were in Smigic, which I -- first of all, Smigic is a neighbourhood within your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and with respect to this neighbourhood, this Smigic or Zmigic, I'm not sure which is the proper pronunciation, approximately how many Serbian civilians were there in this neighbourhood in early 1998 before they all left?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: How could I know? I believe there were 10 or 12 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, isn't it a fact that in -- sometime in 1998, the UCK/KLA, again, in your home village, abducted and murdered several persons from the Zmigic households, that is to say ethnic Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear about that. At that time I was in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you not pay attention to events in your home village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. You know, I wanted to get as far away from the threat as possible. I did not follow the events in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You did not find it odd that 10 or 12 households from your village left in 1998, all around the same time, all of them Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. I didn't find it odd because the Albanians left as well. They went to Montenegro and everywhere they could. It was Albanians, in fact, that left in larger numbers than the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, sir, isn't it a fact that all the Serb civilians of your village left after the UCK, which you said was not really in your village, operated in your village to kill several members of the Smigic household?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And let me again -- let me again refer you to Abedin Draga, and if I put to you that in his sworn statement dated April 12th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's not go down that road. Just put to him what it is you want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question is, if Mr. Draga was there in 1998, Mr. Abedin Draga, if he stated that the area was nominally under the control of the KLA/UCK, you would have no information to debate that, would you? To refute that, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know what the date was, but it was Abedin Draga that was the first one to leave to go to Albania. I don't know what he wrote in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Ms. Carter, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, after speaking with our case manager, it appears the Defence counsel has released no documents pursuant to your discovery -- or, excuse me, your evidence order. The usage of this statement or any statement in reference to the cross-examination of this witness is completely inappropriate, as the proper releases were not given by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in preparing for this cross-examination I had not really intended to posit some of these questions, but the testimony is somewhat different from the statement that was given to us and the Rule 65 ter summary that was given to us from the Office of the Prosecutor regarding what we were to expect to hear here today. So obviously I'm trying to address facts that were brought into evidence based upon the direct testimony of the witness that, thankfully, I happened to have had the luck to stumble upon material that assists me in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not convincing me, Mr. Ivetic. You sound pretty well-prepared for this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what happens when you stay up until 5.00 in the morning preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you anticipate using documents, they should be disclosed. The rule is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm not using this document. I'm positing facts to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different answer, and I think that means now that we quite clearly depart from this idea that you can use the evidence of one person to confront another by referring to his sworn testimony in a statement, which is quite different, in fact, from anything that might have been said in a judicial context. And let's just put the points to the witness that you want him to address, rather than refer to statements which we are -- which have not been logged into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And actually that's -- the last question that I asked was the last one that I had from that -- in that line of questioning, so I can move on. I just have to see whether he's actually answered the question before we departed on this tangent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he did answer, so I will move on to -- for what it's worth, I will move on with the remainder of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in -- earlier today you mentioned an encounter with the Serbian police whereby you claim that they mistreated you, and I believe it was either in 1997 or 1998. In any event, I would ask you to focus on that portion of your testimony. And I would ask you: After that encounter, did you in fact report that conduct to any higher police officials? Did you file a complaint?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Who could I complain to? Do you think that I could go to the people that beat me up, for them to beat me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, the OSCE and other international missions were in Kosovo and Metohija during parts of that time period. Did you ever lodge a complaint with any of these organisations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you aware of a system for complaints being made of this nature to these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or are we really just playing games with this kind of thing? I mentioned the other day the importance of concentrating the cross-examination on what really matters here, and trying to skip the margin -- the things that are of marginal importance. Do you really think that going along this road with this witness is a profitable route to inform the Bench on the issues that we really have to determine in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe notice to the accused is of critical importance in these proceedings and, with respect to events that the Prosecution leads, I think I'm entitled to ask about whether this witness made any type of efforts to provide notice of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you just settle for the first answer and get on? You know he hasn't complained. So why don't we just move on rather than to do all this dancing around these sort of formalities that you and I might consider appropriate in the context, but which is very difficult to imagine the witnesses that we're hearing from would dream of doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On a certain level I agree with you, Your Honour, but I also thought that his statement -- that his sworn statement was very clear, and I've been shown to be otherwise today. So, unfortunately I have to explore areas that I will not focus on but that are of some importance to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that you, like me, were not surprised that the Prosecution had departed from the sworn statement approach in the case of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, and what we're getting is a much more accurate reflection of how this witness is capable of recording events than that statement would ever have given us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it calls into question, Your Honour, the validity and probative value of other statements taken by the Office of the Prosecutor which are being admitted in great number in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, it doesn't. It only -- it only raises issues in relation to this particular witness and to no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will accept those comments, Your Honour, and I'll move on to another portion of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, my examination; the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- one moment. If we could focus on the events in Izbica, and in particular in we could focus on the time period when you stated that the group of men were separated, is it fair to say that there was one individual among these armed forces that separated the group into two groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There wasn't a single person. There were many more than one. There were quite a lot there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the manner in which the group was divided into two. You mentioned an individual whom you said had a black uniform. Is that the man who divided the larger group into two groups, the group you were in and the other group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When they had already separated men from women, that person divided the group of men into two groups, telling one group to go east and the other group to go west.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the man I'm talking about. And I want to ask you: Is it true that there was only this one man who actually divided the groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When they first divided us, they were all there. But this person told us to divide into two groups and lead one group in one direction and the other group in the other direction, and I will never forget this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this person that divided you, you said there were police and other forces there. First, this person who divided you, was he a police officer or something else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't look at him properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that in your testimony today that Milazim was in the other group. Would that be a reference to Milazim Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Milazim was in the group that went west. I was in the group that went east when they divided us at the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware, sir, that Mr. Thaqi testified here for us yesterday and at -- at around the transcript pages --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At around the transcript page 42, line 5 through 7 and 60 -- line 24, he gave a very different description of the nature of the clothing that this gentleman was wearing. Could -- well, do you have any way of reconciling that discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how on earth could he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's true. Let me ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that you did not get a good look at the people that were there with guns in Izbica that are alleged to have done the shooting, and that you therefore don't know what forces they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Milazim was on the side of the men who were told to go in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a different question. In your direct examination you said that the Serb forces that were coming into Izbica included the Serbian police. How is it that you could identify members of the Serbian Ministry of Interior as being among the Serb forces if you could not get a good look at the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I told you once and I am telling you again. I didn't look at the uniform. I know that the police and the army -- the Serbian police and the army came, and I may tell you that I didn't even dare to look at them, have a good look at them or at their clothes. I don't know why you are asking this of me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
