utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is: Upon what do you base the assertion that the police were there? If you don't know, I can move on, just say that you don't know if you truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I am telling you that there was the police and the army and they divided us and then they shot at us. What else can I tell you? I'm telling you the true things of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to move to the burial site. You testified in -- during your direct examination from the Prosecutor's office that there were persons that were killed in May of 1999. Is it a fact that the bodies of those people as well were buried at the same Izbica burial site as the persons that you state were killed on -- in the event that you've described here that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The bodies killed in the massacre were buried in the same place. Also, other people who were shot in other places, and they were buried in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what I'm trying to find out is: Is it not true that persons -- that persons or bodies from several areas over a period of time of several months were collected and buried at the Izbica location, and that these were not all from the same occurrence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The first day of the massacre they were buried at Izbica. Some were killed on the way. The lady who was over 100 years old. On the 11th of May, they killed three; on the 14th of May, they killed 11. They were also buried in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I will take that as a "yes" that bodies from other locations and from other incidents over a span of time of several months were buried in Izbica. Am I accurate in taking that as a yes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Those who were killed in Izbica were buried in Izbica. No other bodies killed elsewhere are brought -- were brought and buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But persons were buried there who -- strike that. Persons were buried there in the months following March of 1999. Is that not accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that, please. Mr. Ivetic, the answer is as plain as day, that that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first one was, but the second one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One has to wonder why you ask the second question. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the persons buried there, were -- do you have knowledge of any UCK fighters that may have been also interned at the Izbica burial grounds with the other people there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, the Office of the Prosecutor asked you about exhumations of the bodies, and I believe you testified that that this place over several dais and during the day-time. Based upon your information relative to these exhumations, were there -- or what type of personnel performed the exhumations? That is to say, were there civilians present for the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I know that it was the Serbian police and army, because they wanted to cover up the traces of the crime. Nobody was interested in coming and exhumating these bodies and taking them to Belgrade or Mitrovica or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified, and it sounded to me like you had quite a bit of knowledge of these exhumations or at least that's the way your testimony was presented to us. So I'm going to ask you: Based upon the information that you had, did it appear that the persons who were exhuming the bodies did not take any efforts to hide their efforts since they were undertaken in the day-time, over a span of several days?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: As -- what I told you is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how or from whom do you have knowledge of the exhumations that were -- that you state were undertaken of the bodies in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: First we learned because of the shelling, and then after three, four days we went to the site and we didn't see a single corpse. They had all been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- sir, I believe in your direct examination you made specific reference to the time of day that the exhumations were carried out and the number of days that it took for the exhumations to be undertaken. From whom or in what manner did you acquire such specific information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Everybody saw that because in the evening they left and we went to the place and saw what had happened when dark fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So are you telling us that all of the testimony that was elicited from you regarding the exhumations is -- that none of that is based upon any direct eye-witness to what transpired; that is to say, nobody told you what they saw with their own eyes the actual process of the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: You can ask for yourself. The -- the corpses of Izbica were found in other places. These are living -- live testimony. They were found in Batajnica, Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, we know that there may be information to that effect, but what counsel is asking you is who told you about the exhumation. And he wants to know if that was a person who actually saw it. Now, can you think about that and think about whether someone who actually saw it told you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gani saw that and then after two, three days, I personally went there, because in the evening they left. And then there -- and I saw it, that there was nobody left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "Gani," could you please provide us with some more information about that. Who is this Gani?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: He's from Izbica. He lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is he a farmer? A civilian? What is he by occupation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: He is a farmer. He used to work as a kind of guard in the school. I don't know if he is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your testimony here today, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm completed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is John Ackerman, along with Aleksander Aleksic, I represent General Pavkovic in this proceeding. I have very, very few questions I want to ask you. I'm going to try to make them as clear as I can. If there is a time that you don't understand the question that I ask you, will you let me know and I'll rephrase it in a way that helps you understand it. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I hope the questions that I ask you can be answered very directly and briefly. I think they can. I'm going to try to ask you questions that can be answered that way. So please try to do that and we'll get through this rapidly. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. During your testimony, at the very beginning this morning, at page 7 you were talking about 25th of March, 1999, when there was some shelling of your village. The question I have is this: You never were able to see, to actually see with your eyes, the persons who were doing the shelling, were you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They were not very far when they started shelling, but the shelling took place and the houses were burned immediately after that. It is called Cetikas [phoen], upper neighbourhood. This is from where they started shelling at, and then they shelled our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see, that was what I was talking about when I spoke to you at the beginning, that I would try to ask you questions that could be answered easily. And obviously you've misunderstood my question. Because I don't contest there was no shelling, which is apparently what you heard. The only thing I want to know from you is, tell me yes or no: You could not see the persons that were actually doing the shelling at the time the shelling was happening, could you? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, but I heard the noise of the shelling. The shells fell in our fields. How could one dare go and see the person who was shelling? They would have done short work of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave a statement to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a -- there is an issue before I go into this that I want to raise. I think I heard Your Honour say this morning that the Prosecution gave you, the Chamber, the Judges, a copy of this witness's statement; and I presume that you have it in English, and if the Prosecution had no intent to admit it in evidence I'm wondering why they gave it to you and what authority they have to give you documents like this when they're not going to use them as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wondered exactly the same thing, Mr. Ackerman, and when I discovered that the witness was to be live, I immediately gave instructions that on all future occasions statements will not be sent to us when it's intended to lead the witness live. And that instructions has already been relayed. The same thing has already happened with one other witness, who was K-62, and it's happened, I think, because she certainly - and I'm not sure about this witness - but certainly K-62 was presented to us initially as a 92 bis witness, and we in fact granted authority for that evidence to be led that way. And we may have done the same with this one. I haven't checked. Maybe Ms. Carter can tell us if that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, no, that is not the same position here. A judgement call was made by the senior trial attorney, who originally was handling this witness, that it appeared from reading old transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, all you need to tell me is, this witness was present -- there was never an application for his evidence under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's happened in both circumstances. I've taken steps to deal with it, and I hope you've judged from the remarks I made earlier about this witness's statement, that I will have absolutely no regard to it or the transcript in the Milosevic trial, except to the extent they may be referred to in the course of his live evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that leads me to -- and thank you, Your Honour, that explains it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think the other Judges received the same. I think I was the only person who -- who actually -- and certainly no one -- no one has read anything except me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really have almost no concern about that with regard to this witness. The next question that I have, though, is: Was this statement put into the system under an exhibit number, the English version of this statement? I know there's an Albanian version in there under an exhibit number, but I don't know if there's an English number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on our witness notification, it appears that there was no exhibit number attached to this package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question, though, that's being asked, Ms. Carter. The question is whether there's an English version in the system as well as an Albanian one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There is an English one. I can give the ERN number, if desired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's whether there's a P number, whether it's actually in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: P2244, I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and Your Honour, I've just looked at P2244, and it's all Albanian, unless there's some -- unless I don't know how to look at it. But there's a 13-page document that's Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can take it, Mr. Ackerman, that this particular Bench will certainly not be going researching the e-court for statements of witnesses who may have given evidence here just to check up on them or for statements that are there that might never have been referred to and might relate to people who never come here. It's the last thing we have time to do, and you have our assurance it will not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm getting where I'm trying to go by a very round about way and I'm confusing you and everyone else. What I'm trying to find out is, if that statement is in the system with an exhibit number, then I have no interest in getting it into the system with an exhibit number because I do want to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's where I'm trying to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got there. It's P2224, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I want it admitted under that P2244 if the English version of that transcript, of that statement is part of that packet, and I can't find that it is. But There's a head nod over there saying it is, and I'm wondering why, when I search for P2224, all I get is a 13-page Albanian document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a measure of confidence, Mr. Ackerman, which will be tested in a moment when you ask for it to come up on the screen that's attached to the Albanian one, which is 2244, are the two translations in B/C/S and English, and therefore if you call up that number you should get an English version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've just displayed my ignorance of the e-court system, Your Honour; that that's the way it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Join the club. Now, just to be absolutely clear, the number is not -- it is 2224. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 2244, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, we need you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you want it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I move its admission. And if you want me to wait until after I have referred to it and used it, then I'll wait until then to move the admission. It's up to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it will be part of the record insofar as you use it; that's our position in relation to exhibits. And that's a fairly normal process with a statement, which I suspect you're going to use to confront the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I just want to use -- I don't want to spend a lot of time in cross-examination confronting him on every item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, and with us you don't need to do that. If you want it admitted in its entirety and the Prosecution take no objection to that, and as long as it's been identified properly, then the Bench would have regard to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- for which you seek it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking. Now, I'll go to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Draga, you spoke to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and gave a statement in November of 1999. Do you recall doing that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that your memory -- your detailed memory of the events that you were describing would have been better seven years ago, or nearly seven years ago, than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. I will always remember the massacre, even in my sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I know that. There are some things about that situation that will remain vivid in your mind forever; that's for sure. But some of the details surrounding what you call this massacre, I suggest to you that you probably remembered a lot better seven years ago than you do today. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I remembered them seven years ago, and I remember them now. And I will always remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Seven years ago when you gave this statement, there was a time at the end of that process when it was read to you in Albanian so you could understand it, and you were asked that everything that was in it was true and correct. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said that this statement was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I said what I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read you a witness acknowledgement, part of one, that appears at the end of the statement that has your signature there, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if this is, again, as productive. I'm sure, Mr. Ackerman, if you have a problem, a technical problem, with this that the Prosecution will stipulate to this being a statement completed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there's no technical problem with that, Your Honour, I just want to make sure that he -- I think I've gotten to where I need to go with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem, as I see it, with this whole thing - and it might as well be addressed now - is witnesses who have been giving evidence here often regard questions of this nature as a challenge to the accuracy of what they've actually said and they don't focus as clearly as we are used to doing on answering the specific point. Now, I'm not suggesting that as a general comment about how they answer questions of every nature; we need to review that later. But I think on this point it's possible to draw conclusions already that what a witness speaking of these events is likely to do here when faced with this sort of question is retell the story and confirm it's accurate. And that's why I'm saying we can perhaps short-circuit this in these cases. It may be different when you're faced with a witness, a professional witness, in a different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that observation is certainly a correct one, and I've made that observation myself. And it -- there is a dilemma as to how to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: The English version of the statement that I have in front of me that has your signature appearing at the bottom of page 3 refers to the forces you saw that day during these events, the 27th and 28th of March, when you said you saw them advancing toward you on foot and the day this event you called the massacre occurred. You said this: "I saw all had the Serbian word 'milicija' on their uniform sleeves near to the shoulder." Now, you told us today that you really didn't notice their uniforms, didn't see the uniforms they were wearing, but in your statement you even identified a word that they had on their sleeves by their shoulder, that all of them had. Can you explain that discrepancy? Can you explain that difference between what you said seven years ago and what you told the Judges here today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know what they wrote in the statement. What I said is that they had police clothes, because as I told you I didn't dare to have a good look at them. And it was the policemen that took us from there to the area where we were executed. They had the milicija uniform, but whether they were milicija or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony here today, I got confused by something you said. It's on page 19. You told the questioner that a 105-year-old man was killed. You were asked the name of that man, and you said it was: Zade Draga, a woman. Was there just a misunderstanding? Did you always say it was a woman or did you first say it was a man and then change it to a woman when you were asked the name? I don't -- I just got confused by that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: That person was a woman. Maybe a mistake was made. Maybe I was misunderstood. I won't forget her; she lived in my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that Zade Draga was a woman who lived in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was 105 years old?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, 105 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that in a schedule submitted by the Prosecutor to this Trial Chamber in the indictment of people that were killed at Izbica, the -- there is a Zade Dragaj, 71-year-old male. Do you know a Zade Dragaj who was a 71-year-old male?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So would it be your testimony that when the Prosecutor informed the Chamber that Zade Dragaj, a 71-year-old male, was killed at Izbica, that that was misinformation, that that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, that would call for speculation on behalf of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It calls for no speculation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, it's unlikely to get a helpful answer nevertheless. Might it not be better to approach this from the point of view of gender and the -- what -- what's the likely gender of the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the point is made, Your Honour. I don't think it needs any further elaboration, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about a few KLA being in your village, and the Judge even questioned you about it, before the shelling started, that there were a few KLA in your village. I want to ask you just a couple of questions about those KLA. Did the KLA that were in your village wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, the ones that were with the KLA had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Some of them did. Some of them didn't carry weapons. They did not have enough weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did they sometimes wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I did not see them in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what did they do as the Serb forces approached your village? Did they fight them or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you know where they went, tell me; if you don't know where they went, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know where they left. I was not with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Now, what -- what I understand you want the Chamber to do is to admit the statement in its entirety in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do, otherwise I would have to spend the next 30 minutes going through the parts of it that I would like to draw your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what you have in mind is in due course to draw -- in submissions to draw the Chamber's attention to discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's much more efficient, Your Honour, unless you disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, the statement is admitted in full in this case, albeit it was referred to only to a limited extent. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will act accordingly to what you have just agreed with Mr. Ackerman, and I will seize of this opportunity to point out to some discrepancies at a later stage. All I, therefore, have to do is pose a couple of questions of the witness, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, one of the counsel for Vladimir Lazarevic. At the beginning of your testimony you said you have eight sons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During the relevant period, as regarding this indictment, this being 1998 and 1999, your sons, to a large extent, were already grown up and they were able-bodied. They could serve the military. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Apart from that, I believe you stated today that indeed there were KLA members in your village. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following, Mr. Draga, did members of the KLA ask of you or of any of your sons, since they were able-bodied, to join them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, they did not join because they did not have weapons. If they had had weapons, probably they would have joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Draga, your sons were asked to join, but they did not since they didn't have any weapons. Is this the way we should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know that they were asked to join. I know that they did not have guns, so they just did not volunteer to go because they did not have guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Had they had rifles, they would have joined the KLA for sure. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got that answer twice already, Mr. Bakrac. Please move on. We have to develop some more efficient method of cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, didn't you in your testimony a while ago say that in 1997 a weapon was taken by the police from you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I said that I was taken to the police station, but I did not have a gun to give them. I said it earlier; I'm saying it now again. If I had the gun, they wouldn't beat me; they just would have taken the gun and left me alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, you did not have any weapon prior to 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, you spoke about your participation in the burial of the 147 men -- people. Since you participated in their burial, I'd like to know the following. Were these all elderly people or were there some young people among them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were some young people. Hajriz Draga, for example, he was 40 years old. There were people from Klina and Skenderaj and other places who were young.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, a bit earlier in your testimony you said that only elderly men stayed behind and that the younger men had taken to the woods. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It is true that the majority of us were old people, but there are -- there were some that were young. I've come here to tell the truth. I'm not here to tell lies. I don't know why you are making me here appear as if I'm telling lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, my job here is to ascertain the truth, and I wanted to ask for your assistance. I am not clear as to which of the two is correct. You said that only elderly people remained and that younger people went to the woods, and then these elderly were shot dead. But now we hear that among the 147 there were quite -- there were some younger people as well. Were there any KLA fighters among the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There was no one from the KLA killed in the massacre of Izbica. There were some teachers. I wouldn't call them elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, we saw here that even some professors were members of the KLA, so the mere fact that these people were teachers doesn't necessarily tell us anything about their membership with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The teacher was killed; he wasn't a member of the KLA. Had he been a member of the KLA, he wouldn't have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Draga. I have only one question left. If I understood you correctly, the exhumation for which you stated you heard was carried out by the Serbian police and the MUP, that exhumation was carried out at day-time and they were shelled. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I told you earlier and I am telling you again, when they wanted to come and exhume the corpses, they first shelled the area and then went into the site. And when the shelling started, we knew that they would do that. It was exactly there that they took the corpses from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But first they shelled the location from which they took the bodies. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I repeat it again and that is true. Because everything they did, they shelled first and then they did what they had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You needn't repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have but one question, and that is again -- is again concerning the notice. There were things that I learned only after having entered the courtroom, and I strongly object to the OTP continuing to do so in spite of your previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Toma Fila, and together with my learned friend Mr. Petrovic I appear here on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. The only question I have is regarding the exhumation that has just been discussed. Since I wasn't able to prepare myself for the cross-examination, I wanted to remind everyone here that among the material received by the OTP, we received a report provided upon the request of the OTP, and the court in Kosovo Mitrovica attempted to carry the exhumation discussed here. Were you familiar with such a fact that the local court attempted to exhume those bodies but was unsuccessful because the exhumation team was shelled. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. I don't know what they would look for there because it was themselves that did it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila should wait for the English interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you whether you knew that the court attempted to do that. That's all I wanted to know. Another question concerning that. You said that after that you went to the place of the incident and that you were able to establish that all the bodies were taken away. That was approximately two months after they were buried, the 25th or the 28th of March. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, between the 25th of March and the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because at the place where those bodies had been buried at the time when you went there, the bodies were no longer there. There was nothing to indicate that some bodies had previously been buried there or was there anything?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know that before the 31st of March, there was no cemetery there. And the whole meadow was used to bury those people who were killed there. And the people collected all the bodies and buried them there, and I take full responsibility when I say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. What I am asking you is the following: Once the shelling stopped and after the exhumation operation was concluded, you said you went there and that you saw it with your own eyes, that there was not a single buried body there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that and I can repeat it if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the next question is this: At that place where there were no more corpses, did you see anything that would indicate that there had been some bodies there? Did you find any traces? Anything?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We found clothes. We found a cut hand. The clothes of the people who had been buried there were on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, a hand and some clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A hand and clothes, and I didn't want to look any further. It was gruesome.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will conclude with this topic, but I do have another question. Do you have any knowledge of the Serbian language? Can you understand it at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, no, I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you served your military term, what was the main language used?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: In Srpska, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But now you tell us you don't understand any Serbian. Have you forgotten it in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, at that time I did not know the language very well. It was in the 1960s, and I forgot everything I had learned even then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I say "good morning" or "good afternoon," do you know what it means in Serbian, "dobar dan"? Do you have at least some basics? Good afternoon? Bye?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, I've forgotten them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, then, just one last question. In which language did the policemen address you when he told you to split into two groups and in which language did he curse your mothers, since you say you don't understand Serbian? That would be my last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: He was cursing us in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our jurisdiction, Your Honour, attorneys cannot comment; therefore, I need to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They shouldn't be commenting in this jurisdiction either, Mr. Fila. Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one brief point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, you indicated that there was a gentleman by the name of Shaban Draga who was present during the burials. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. I said earlier that Shaban Draga was not there at the burial site. I only told you that I know Shaban Draga as a person, but not that he was there at the burial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the one and only Shaban Draga that you know is an older man, not somebody in his 20s. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, he is an elderly person. I don't know how old he is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the allusion I anticipate being drawn in -- with regards to this gentleman is: Is he now or was he ever a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd also like to ask you a little bit about your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution. At the time that your statement was taken as well as the time that you were going through the 92 bis procedures, was your statement read out to you in order for you to understand what was contained in it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the time that it was read out to you, did they take it paragraph by paragraph, asking you questions about individual pieces? Or were you read an entire statement all in one go and then asked to comment in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No, they read the whole statement at one go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. If there are small discrepancies within the statement, is that a function of -- that you were read an entire statement all at once and did not understand that there were discrepancies there, or were you making notes for yourself? What did you do in order to do the proofing procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's excessively leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not only is it excessively leading, it's argumentative, it's a submission, it's quite inappropriate at this stage in the examination of the witness, so I sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafa, I have a question for you. You said that the people who gave money to those who were asking for it were spared. You did not have any money, you did not give any money. How did they spare you then? This is my first question. Or how did you save yourself then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, I think it was God that saved me and Hajriz Draga that fell on me, because even other people they could see were still alive, they were killed. There were people who paid money and they were still killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Before burying of the bodies, was any ritual performed or they were just inserted in holes or depressions or graves? You said each was put in a different grave. That must have taken a long time. Can you please comment on all what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It was a good area. The field was soft soil, so it was easy for us to dig the graves. People were happy to give them a proper burial in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Draga, that concludes -- that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in connection with the last part of the re-direct examination of the Prosecutor, I would respectfully refer Your Honours to the last page of the statement that's now in evidence as P2244, the interpreter certification, and would ask the Prosecution if it is now their position that the interpreter certification is incorrect and was wrongly certified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're taking no issue with the interpreter's certification on the statement, but rather the fact that when somebody is read eight pages all at one time and then asked about minor details within it, that's going to be a little bit difficult. That was the point of the examination, not to cause any damage to the interpretation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's going to be a matter of some debate where the discrepancies are minor or not, and that's for a later stage. I think you have the basic position, Mr. Ackerman, that the Prosecution adhere to that as a statement that was taken as it is presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- the next thing I wonder after what was just told you is: Is this a standard procedure that's used in the taking of these statements? Is no care taken to make sure that the witness understands what the statement says? That they speed through it, reading it, and say: Sign it. If that's what they do, then we shouldn't have any statements admitted at all in this case because they have no reliability at all, period. If they do it more carefully, then they do it more carefully, but I think now we need to know how they do this. Is there a procedure or do they just speed through these translations with no care?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the weakness of your submission on that submission is that the Prosecution have not relied on this statement, and they have obviously done that in relation to one particular statement for their own reasons, and I think we can all see that these may well have been sound reasons. It doesn't follow for one minute that that undermines every other statement that's led. And as you know you've been given the opportunity and will be given the opportunity to cross-examine every witness whose evidence is provided by statement so far. There may yet be issues on which it's not necessary for a witness to attend here, that remains to be seen, but so far we have decided they all should. In these circumstances, their statement can be challenged. It's also open to you to make inquiry -- further inquiry of the Prosecution, if you wish to, to go into this matter in more detail and investigate it. And that's a matter you're entirely free to raise with the Prosecution. But it's not something clearly that we can take any stand on in the light of the presentation of the evidence -- the statement of one witness on which there may be substantial criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if this interpreter, Beznik Sokali, is available in any way, I think either the Court or I should inquire of her, if that's exactly what she did, was read it through in such speed that the person couldn't understand what she was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter I encourage you to take up direct. That's not a matter for us at this point. Now the next witness, Ms. Carter, is -- or Mr. Hannis is -- can you give us an indication of how long it's anticipated that this witness will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had estimated that it might take me 45 minutes on direct. I don't know if you're aware, Your Honour, we proposed to proceed with this witness as a 92 bis (D) using her transcript from the Milosevic testimony and also a recently prepared 89(F) statement, rather than the 92 bis package that was previously submitted. Upon proofing her yesterday, we discovered that -- it appeared to me to be somewhat confusing, the chronology in that written statement, so we prepared a new statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The previous testimony, did that incorporate the statement she had previously given?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. We have furnished the Defence a track-changes version, showing where we have made changes, where there are some new items, and in other places where material has just been shifted from one paragraph to another to make the chronology read in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when you tender the transcript, so far you've told me that that automatically incorporates any exhibit, and in relation to these transcripts that has generally been the statement that the witness was making which was a previous 92 bis statement. Now, are you saying that in this case we have to -- or in fact, was she previously a 92 bis witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A 92 bis (D), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but in the -- Milosevic, was she -- yeah, she was. She was a 92 bis witness in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would say if you were following the practice you've followed so far that when you tender her transcript that automatically brings in her statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now telling me you don't want the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not in this case; however, Your Honour, this -- we have -- the transcript has one Exhibit Number, P2226, or 2260. I'm sorry, 2260, and the written statements that were -- the 92 bis (B) package in Milosevic has the number 2259. We're proposing to tender with this witness 2260, which is the testimony, not tender 2259, but rather tender a new exhibit, the 89(F) statement that she signed this morning to be given a number at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And so the accused are only now receiving this 89(F) statement, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Last night we advised them that this was my intention, to proceed this way, when we were discussing the order of witnesses, whether she would be next or whether the doctor from this municipality would be next. It appeared there was a preference among everyone to have her appear next. I expressed my difficulty and my dilemma with the 48-hour rule regarding 89(F) statements, and the Defence indicated to me, under the circumstances, they were willing to give me a one-time agreement to proceed in that fashion. And, Your Honour, given the hour that we're at and my estimated time on direct, it's likely that any cross-examination may not begin until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is this a witness who is likely to be cross-examined at length? Does any have an idea that this may take some time? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it would take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll adjourn now and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Xhafa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated, and please make yourself comfortable before we begin. Now, we do have before us in writing a statement of things you have to tell the Tribunal. We also have a copy of what you said when you gave evidence before in another trial here. So we already know a great deal about what you can say of the events that we are dealing with. The purpose of the hearing today is to allow the counsel who represent the Prosecution and the various accused to ask you additional questions, and hopefully these will be very specific questions. So please do your best to listen carefully to the question asked and to answer the particular question each time. And the first person to ask you questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I indicated before the break, we intend to proceed with this witness as a combination of a 92 bis (D) witness, her transcript which is 2260, 6-0, and an 89(F) statement which was signed today and does not yet have an exhibit number. We have English and B/C/S versions at this time which have been provided to Defence counsel. And to the Court, I believe you have the English copies. An Albanian translation has been requested but not received yet, and we would ask that that statement be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that will be the next Prosecution number, which is, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that 2274, 2274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can the court deputy confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would indicate, Your Honours, that the evidence of this witness refers primarily to paragraph 72 (M), as in Michael, paragraph 73 regarding forcible transfer, paragraph 75 (I), and paragraph 76 and 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you state your full name for us?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: My name is Fedrije Xhafa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Xhafa, I understand from your statement that in 1999 you were living in the municipality of Vushtrri or Vucitrn. Can you tell us the name of your village?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Lower Saracak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And about how big was your village.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It has approximately 80 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does it have a different name now than it did in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes. Now we call it Mans i Ulet [phoen], lower Mans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Xhafa, before coming to court today to testify, earlier this week did you have a chance to meet with representatives from my office to go over your prior written statements in this case?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: This week, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of doing that, did you bring to the attention of my office some -- some details that you wanted to add and some changes that you felt should be made to those written statements?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this time, if I could hand a hard copy of Exhibit 2274, an English version, to the witness. I just want to ask her a couple of questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Xhafa, could you -- I realise that document is in English. Do you speak and understand any English?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I speak a little. I understand a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at that document and look at each page and see if you recognise what it is, even though it is in English.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at what's in handwriting on each of those pages?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is then based on your review?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: That's my signature after making some changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And earlier this morning, was that -- was that statement regarding the changes read back to you in Albanian by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you satisfied that what was read out to you accurately reflected the changes that you wanted made to your prior statement?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that then accurately reflect to the best of your knowledge and memory the truth about the events you describe in that statement?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects them accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 2274 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Xhafa, as the Judge indicated, they do have this written document plus your prior testimony in the Milosevic case, so I'll try to go quickly through your statement and ask you about a few specific points. In paragraph 2 of that statement, Ms. Xhafa, you describe how on the 28th of March, 1999, you and your family left your home because Serb forces had begun to burn houses in your village. Where did you go from your village?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: From our village we went on the 28th of March, and it was a sunny day -- it was Sunday. We went to Dumnica village. There I stayed one day. On the next day, we set out from Dumnica to Samodreza, where I stayed for a very brief time. And then we continued our way until we arrived at Vesekovc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The day you left on the 28th, when you say Serb forces were beginning to burn houses, did you actually see them doing that yourself?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They started to set fire to all the houses in upper Saracak, and therefore all the villagers began to leave the village. We, too, joined them. It was very dangerous to remain in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you describe anything about the forces that were doing this in terms of uniform or equipment or weapons, from what you can see?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Like all the others, my village started -- my village started to be emptied of its population. We had Serbian neighbours, and they left the village and went to Drenakovc [phoen] village. And they fired with heavy weapons. I don't know what kind of weapons they were, we weren't told. So we began to be afraid. As I said, the houses also began to be set on fire. That's why we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But were you able to see the persons who were doing this and see what kind of uniforms they were wearing, if any?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No. They were very far away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 4 of your statement, you say that around the 30th of April your family travelled from Vesekovc to Sllakoc. Am I pronouncing that close to right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you spent two nights there, and you were informed by KLA fighters that Serb forces were coming in your direction from the north, and then you and your family joined a large convoy of people moving towards Vushtrri or Vucitrn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then further on in paragraphs 5 to 9 you describe what happened on the 2nd of May while you were in the convoy. And I think you describe four different times that different Serb forces, I think in most cases they were described as policemen, approached your convoy and had dealings with your family, including the last encounter [Realtime transcript read in error, "country"] in which your brother, Jetish, was shot and your father was shot and killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your father's name and how old was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Miran, and he was 71 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your brother, Jetish, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: At the time he was 45 years, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he actually survive that shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But at the time, you were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No. We thought he was dead and continued on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 20 on page 80, what Mr. Hannis said was "the last encounter" and not "the last country." In the normal course of things, I should point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thanks for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When and how did you discover that your brother had survived that shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We realised that on the 7th of May when some acquaintances of ours came to Kciq village and they told someone from there that village. I think it was a woman of some 30 years old. I don't remember her name. She came to the house we were staying in and she told us that he was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: After the war was over. It was the 16th of June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he confirm to you at that time what had happened to your father, whether or not he had survived as well?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: He didn't know -- we didn't tell him for a while. He thought he was in Albania together with the mother. Then after a week or so, we told him the truth, namely that the father was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you tell us in your statement after -- after that happened, the policemen told you to drive on down the road. Your family went down the road a little ways, and then eventually you abandoned your tractor and your belongings. Why did you do that? Why did you leave things behind?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We were obliged to do that, because if we remained in the tractor we felt great risk because police would come up to the people staying on the tractors and beat them. Someone was passing by told us, it's better for us to leave than remain in the tractor. That's why we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You then go on in your statement to tell us how you made your way to the outskirts of Vushtrri, where you were directed by police to go to what's described as an agricultural co-op building, and you spent the night there. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your statement says: The next morning the men between the ages of 15 and 60 were separated and taken off to prison, that those people who had tractors were told to go to Albania, and the rest of you were directed to go to -- can you help me with the name of the town where you were told to go?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Those were taken -- the men were taken to [Realtime transcript read in error, "from"] the prison of Smrekonica, whereas we, the rest, were directed to go to Smrekonic or Kciq village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were you told to do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We stayed there in a house, in Kciq.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when the -- when the -- the war ended, the fighting ended and NATO came, did you return to your original home?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We returned after two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What condition was it in?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The house was burned down, and we had to put up a tent where we stayed in the courtyard of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like next to show you an exhibit. It's P38. This is a map that will come up on your computer screen in a moment, and when it does I would like to ask the usher to help hand you an electronic pen that's attached to the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's another transcript problem that I think should be pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Line 20 -- page 82, line 23, the witness didn't say the men were taken from the prison, she said they were taken to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you have the map on the screen in front of you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in a bit on the upper half or the upper two-thirds. We're going to try to make it a little more bigger so you may be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it bigger for you yet?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yeah, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My screen is a little slower. Are you able to see your home village on that map?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you -- could you draw a small circle around it and put a number 1 inside the circle?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But -- okay. Thank you. All right. And you mentioned you went first to Dumnica. I don't know that that appears on the map here, but you went then after that to Samodreza. Could you draw a circle around Samodreza and put the number 2 inside it.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I can't Dumnica here, but I can see Samodreza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you draw the circle around Samodreza and put a number 2 by it.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can see Vesekovc on the map that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Can you show us -- can you show us where the convoy was at the time your father and brother were shot? Do you know what two towns it was between at that time on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We were between Studime i Eperme and Studime i Poshtme, somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you would write the number 3 there and draw a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could indicate on this map as well where the -- the prison was or the town you referred to as the prison and where you went to register your new residence. I think it's Smrekonica?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, the prison was in Smrekonica, and it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you put the number 4 inside that circle.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic is up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask my learned friend to point out in the statement of this witness where she mentioned the prison she registered. I think that in the statement it says dispensary or a hospital mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence has been that men were taken off to a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't mean that she went to a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the women, as you say, Mr. Lukic, went to a place in Smrekonica to register.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, that's in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whether -- yes. If you look at paragraph 11, in the fourth line you'll see: "I later learned that all the men were taken to Smrekonica prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, one more for me, if you would, Ms. Xhafa. Could you write the number 5 and draw a circle around Dobar Luka, where you say you stayed.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give that the next IC exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Next IC exhibit number will be IC20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Xhafa, in Dobar Luka, in what house were you and your family staying at? I mean, did you know who lived in that house before you?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the house of Sadi Shala, an inhabitant of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnicity of that village was before the fighting started in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: They were Albanian. All of them were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what had happened to the people who had been living in the village before you came to stay there?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes. Some people had remained in the village, and they told us that the people had been sent to Albania. They had crossed the border. They were in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify one thing for me, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Attached to the 89(F) statement that I've been given are certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. I believe you have a document that is the registration form in Albanian, an original form with handwriting on it, an English translation of the blank form, and you also have what purports to be photographs of various camouflage types which is extremely well camouflaged because all you can see are four black squares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those are intended to be attached, Your Honour. They were part of -- they were part of the 92 bis statement that was part of her transcript. And the camouflage photos, we are attempting to locate the original colour versions that were introduced, I believe, as Exhibit 18 in the Milosevic trial, but all we've been able to obtain anywhere from the registry and from our own files has been a copy just like that one. We are making our best efforts to find a colour version so it will make some sense to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We'll proceed in this order: General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Xhafa, I'm Tomislav Visnjic, representing General Ojdanic. I will be putting some questions to you. Mrs. Xhafa, you gave statements to the OTP investigators in 2001, in 2002, and just immediately prior to coming here about the events that you gave evidence about here today. My question is: Did you also give a statement to someone else, to another organ, including authorities about these events, the murder of your father and the wounding of your brother?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't give any statements to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the territory of your municipality, there is a war crimes commission, an Albanian commission?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You did not talk to them about these events, did you?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I did not have the time, to tell you the truth, because I work full-time. So I did not meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any members of your family perhaps talked to any authorities about these events?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Perhaps. I have not asked anyone about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Xhafa. Now, please tell me, Mrs. Xhafa --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I would like to ask to have IC20 displayed in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is the map, Mrs. Xhafa, the one that you saw just a bit ago, and the one on which you marked certain locations. We can't see it on this map, but based on what I understood in your evidence you joined the convoy in a location called Slakovce. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We started from Sllakoc, and then we entered the village of Studime. It was at the edge of Studime i Eperme.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me, please, we can't see Slakovce on this map, but how far is it from Gornje Studime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we showed P38 without the exhibit without being blown up, I think we may be able to see more, if that will assist counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. I was going to prepare a map for the witness for Monday. I didn't know that this particular copy would be used, but we can try and proceed with this one. What did Mr. Hannis say, I think he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can get away from the IC one and go back to P38 and we get it to a reasonable size for the witness to identify the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, let's blow it up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more time, please, and that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Xhafa, can you see Slakovce on the map?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your view, how far is Slakovce from Gornja Sudimlja, do you have any idea about the distance?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I don't know, to tell you the truth. We went from Sllakoc to Ceceli first, but then from Ceceli we went to the village of Sudimlja. From Ceceli to Sudimlja I think it was about 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you went from Slakovce to Ceceli first, and then from there to Sudimlja. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: There was a road between Sllakoc and Ceceli. We passed through a hilly area, and then went to Studime. I think that the whole route from Sllakoc to Ceceli to Studime i Eperme was about 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that in the convoy, in your view, there were approximately 50.000 people; that was your assessment I assume, right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: That's what I thought. 30.000, 50.000. This is an approximate number, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at any rate it was a column which was continuous basically from Slakovce to as far in front of you as you could see, correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very long column, and in the hill of Studime, I had the opportunity to have a look. I could see from Studime i Eperme to Studime i Ulet, the lower Studime, I could see the people walking, some of them on tractors and cars. It was a very long column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's the column that you saw in front of you, correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but there were people behind us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to clarify this. I suppose that this is some sort of a misunderstanding, but in the Milosevic transcript on page 4148, there is something that I'd like to clarify. Based on your best recollection, when did you join the column in Slakovce?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will go back. You testified in the Milosevic case, at which time you said that you didn't join the column immediately but that rather you waited for some time. And then later in the day you joined the column in Slakovce. Could you please tell us, what time of the day was it when you and your family joined the column?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It was the 2nd of May, in the afternoon. That was the day when we joined the column, and there were so many people in that column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is: What time in that day did you join the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the afternoon, probably about 1.00 or 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when did you arrive in Sudimlja, what time it was?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: At 4.00 p.m., in the afternoon of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, if you want to complete this matter, please do, and then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have three more questions. I don't think that I will overstep the regular hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When discussing the place where you stopped, where you arrived, as you said, at about 4.00, that is actually a location between Gornja and Donja Sudimlja, correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one more question for today. Tell me, please, in the trailer -- this has to do with paragraph 4 of your statement. In the trailer which was attached to the tractor, you said that your entire family was in that tractor. I will ask you only about the males in your family and I will read out the names to make sure I understood it well. In addition to your father who was with you, there was also brothers Jetish, Fazil, and Fazil's three sons, Ismet, who at the time had -- was 20 years old; Lavdim, who was 13; and Mirsad, who was 16 at the time?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, no, you're wrong. On the tractor were these people: Jetish, my father, Ismet, Lavdim. Mirsad and Fazil were walking. Ismet, Mirsad, and Lavdim are Jetish's sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So Mirsad and Fazli walked next to tractor, but they were with you, correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Fazli was walking, he was on foot. They left earlier and they were on foot. We left a little bit later, an we took the tractor. That's what the police told us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you meet them in Donja Sudimlja, where you stopped to rest, as you stated in your statement given on the 2nd of May, 2000?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, we met them. We met Mirsad and Fazli, and we continued on our way all together on foot, up to Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I explored this sufficiently for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Now, Ms. Xhafa, we have to conclude the proceedings for today at this time. We will have to resume again on Monday. Your evidence will continue then. That will be at 9.00 on Monday. You should be back here in time to start giving evidence again at 9.00. Meanwhile, it's very important that over the weekend you do not discuss your evidence with anyone at all, anyone, and that means you don't discuss either the evidence you have already given or the evidence you may yet give in the case. You can talk of anything else, but please, please avoid talking about the evidence. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will see you again at 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24
